C48.mvd: After Alex rolls back a release of five real MRs and assigns the flow, it opens one-change re-land MRs in a chosen order; each deploys to Cloud Run with a short error watch, the fourth brings a planted error back and is held as the suspect, and the rest return.

C49.blocker: Reading pipeline schedules and their next run times through the flow's tools (which API reads the flow token reaches is unverified).
C49.fallback: Keep schedules as code (the schedule list and Cloud Scheduler config in the repo) and run the dry run in the sandbox with the clock set to the next run.
C49.mvd: Alex merges 'change tax rounding'; the flow finds that the monthly invoice job will run the new code for the first time on Sunday at 00:00 and posts it on a next-turn issue, Alex replies 'dry run', the job runs against a staging copy with the clock set to Sunday, three invoices fail, and the fix merges on Friday.

C50.blocker: Load-testing the Cloud Run service honestly from CI: the skeleton caps max instances at 1, and quotas and cold starts make results noisy.
C50.fallback: Test a separate labelled staging revision at a small, stated scale, and make the defense a cache MR whose effect shows at that scale.
C50.mvd: Alex opens a labelled campaign issue with three links and assigns the flow; it maps them to routes, a CI load test on staging shows the promo page failing at 120 requests per second against a 350 estimate, the flow's cache MR is merged, and the rerun passes.

C51.blocker: Running the default-branch pipeline with a route that skips deferred jobs: the route has to reach the protected main pipeline as variables or a committed file.
C51.fallback: The flow commits route.yml to the fix MR, CI rules read it on main, and the deploy job then triggers the full pipeline through the job token; the slow stage is a labelled stand-in.
C51.mvd: During a planted checkout outage Alex mentions the flow on the one-line fix MR; it proposes an 11-minute route that defers the end-to-end suite, code accepts it against never-skip.yml, the fix deploys to Cloud Run, and the full pipeline runs right after and goes green.

C52.trap_reason: The freeze levers (deploy freezes, pausing schedules, cancelling other people's auto-merge) need Maintainer; with a marker file it only pauses jobs we wrote.
C52.blocker: Creating a deploy freeze and pausing pipeline schedules through the API, which needs Maintainer.
C52.fallback: A pause marker that our deploy and rollout jobs check before acting, with the flow doing the inventory and the resume order.
C52.mvd: During a planted incident Alex types '@pause'; the flow lists two pipelines about to deploy, an auto-merge MR and a flag step, the pause marker stops them with a note to each author, and '@pause resume' lets them back one at a time in the proposed order.

C53.blocker: The pipeline events trigger firing on a pipeline that passed after a person's retry, and the flow reading both attempts' job logs.
C53.fallback: Alex mentions the flow with the pipeline link; the experiments run in the flow sandbox with the standard library, or as a manual CI job whose log the flow reads.
C53.mvd: Alex retries a failed checkout test until the pipeline turns green; the flow compares the two logs, runs the experiment (200 isolated runs pass, 200 parallel runs fail 7 times) and opens an issue, 'not flaky: a race in reserve_stock, about 1 in 500 orders would be charged twice', with the reproduction command.

C54.blocker: Rotating the leaked key: a flow cannot read provider credentials, so rotation must be a keyless CI job on main for a key we own.
C54.fallback: Leak a labelled demo key for our own Cloud Run service kept in Secret Manager; the rotation job adds a new secret version and redeploys, and the misuse check reads Cloud Logging.
C54.mvd: Alex pushes a commit containing a labelled demo key; secret detection flags it, the flow opens an incident and asks for containment, after Alex's 'go' a CI job rotates the key and redeploys, the flow reports no use of the old key in the logs, and leaves a no-blame note.

C55.blocker: Pipelines from a person-owned schedule must count as a human action for the pipeline events trigger (unverified), and the scheduled job must deploy from the protected default branch.
C55.fallback: The scheduled job checks code-only conditions itself and deploys when they hold; the flow turns her words into the order on a mention and writes the fill note when she mentions it later.
C55.mvd: Alex writes a limit order on a merged MR and leaves; a schedule he owns checks the real incident state and error rate every 15 minutes, the timeline shows 'incident still open' and 'errors 2.1%', and once both clear the scheduled job deploys to Cloud Run and his phone shows 'order filled'.

C56.blocker: Reading package metadata and publisher history from outside GitLab inside the flow sandbox (allowed domains, strict mode unverified).
C56.fallback: A CI job fetches release age, publisher and diff facts into a log or artifact the flow reads; cooldowns are shortened and labelled, and a person merges instead of auto-merge into protected main.
C56.mvd: Alex starts a rating run over six real dependency bump MRs; the flow fills the rating form from CI-gathered facts, code rates them, the top-rated ones merge after a labelled short cooldown, and a labelled staged package that adds a network-calling install script is blocked with a short report.

C57.blocker: Reading failed requests per account from Cloud Logging needs keyless Google access from CI on main, since the flow cannot reach Google.
C57.fallback: A CI job pulls the incident window's failed orders and prints per-account impact for the flow, and the drafted messages stay as comments on the incident instead of Service Desk email.
C57.mvd: After a planted 40-minute checkout fault hits labelled synthetic customer traffic, Alex closes the incident and assigns the flow; code computes the affected accounts and credits from sla.yml, and the flow drafts one message per account ('your 3 orders failed between 14:02 and 14:41; we sent them again and added a $12 credit') for Alex to approve.

top10_feasible_and_human.why: Runs entirely in the flow sandbox and CI on a labelled synthetic table with no Maintainer setting, and one customer's name mangled on every invoice is the scene.
Hangs on the deploy skeleton's existing manual job, code checks the cited line from a release-tag diff, and one approver catching a debug value at 18:00 is a clear moment.
A real dependency bump and a test that passes on the old lockfile and fails on the new one need no seeded history; a weekend maintainer clears her queue before her coffee cools.
The strongest feeling in the pool (the phone stays dark); day and morning steps use human triggers, and the night step can run as plain code on Cloud Run if the Flows API fails.
'Button, button, button' is the most memorable scene in the pool, and if no browser runs in the sandbox a CI job still produces the transcript and audio honestly.
A planted canary person and a marker search give a yes or no answer that runs in CI; a woman relying on account deletion to stay safe is the human stake.
The dry-run set must equal the set the customer marked, which is simple code, and 'Site mismatch: 11 rows, 1 marked' is a refusal a viewer remembers.
Needs only MR triggers, a WHY.yml file and an upstream issue on gitlab.com; a successor reading the departed author's own words beside a ready MR is warm and specific.
Human triggers throughout and a fault toggle we own in the demo app; a new hire walks into his first on-call week having already done it once.
Drift is read with rights the deploy account already has and the person-started deploy failure starts the flow; a 2 a.m. console fix is saved in its author's name instead of erased.
